cards.b: Proteins involved in all metabolic reactions, functioning as biological catalysts. They are not used up.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged at the end.
The part of an enzyme with a specific shape where the substrate binds.

cards.f: Name the steps of enzyme action
cards.b: Substrate fits the active site → enzyme–substrate complex forms → reaction happens → product(s) released; enzyme unchanged.
Only a substrate with a shape complementary to the active site fits, so each enzyme catalyses one type of reaction.

cards.f: Describe the effect of temperature on enzyme activity
cards.b: Activity rises to a maximum at the optimum temperature, then falls rapidly at higher temperatures.

cards.f: Explain the rise in rate below the optimum temperature
cards.b: More kinetic energy, so more frequent effective collisions and more enzyme–substrate complexes per second.
The active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits. It is permanent.

cards.f: Does a low temperature denature enzymes?
cards.b: No. They are just slow (little kinetic energy) and work again when warmed.

cards.f: Optimum pH of stomach protease versus intestinal amylase
cards.b: Stomach protease: acidic, about pH 2 (hydrochloric acid). Amylase and lipase in the small intestine: slightly alkaline / neutral.

cards.f: Explain the effect of pH away from the optimum
cards.b: The active site changes shape, the substrate fits less well, fewer complexes form; extreme pH denatures the enzyme.

cards.f: Amylase investigation: what is the end point?
cards.b: Iodine drop stays orange-brown, meaning no starch is left. Record the time.

cards.f: How do you calculate rate from time in an enzyme experiment?
cards.b: Rate = 1 ÷ time (or 1000 ÷ time). A shorter time means a faster rate.

cards.f: Why equilibrate enzyme and substrate in a water bath before mixing?
cards.b: So both are at the test temperature when the reaction starts.

cards.f: Suitable control for an amylase experiment
cards.b: Boiled (denatured) amylase, or water instead of amylase. It shows the enzyme causes the change.

short.q: Explain why an enzyme will only catalyse one type of reaction. [2]
short.model: Only one substrate has a shape complementary to the enzyme's active site, so only that substrate fits and forms an enzyme–substrate complex.
points: active site has a specific shape
only a substrate with complementary shape fits / forms enzyme–substrate complex

short.q: Explain why the rate of an enzyme reaction falls to zero at 80 °C. [3]
short.model: The enzyme is denatured: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits, and no enzyme–substrate complexes form.
points: substrate no longer fits / no complexes formed

short.q: Explain why an enzyme in a tube at 5 °C works slowly. [2]
short.model: Enzyme and substrate molecules have little kinetic energy, so there are few effective collisions and few enzyme–substrate complexes.
points: low kinetic energy / molecules move slowly
fewer effective collisions so fewer complexes

short.q: Starch and amylase are mixed. Describe how you would find the time taken for all the starch to be broken down. [3]
short.model: Take a drop of mixture every 30 s and add it to iodine on a spotting tile. When the iodine stays orange-brown no starch is left; record the time.
points: sample at regular intervals onto iodine

short.q: Suggest two variables to control in an experiment on how pH affects amylase. [2]
short.model: Temperature and the volume and concentration of starch and amylase (also sampling interval).
points: same volume / concentration of enzyme and substrate
